When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

issues.explanation: The profile only includes Memory and Negative Appraisals, with the formulation showing a strong reciprocal link specifically between these two nodes. The memory items are dominated by trauma-recall qualities and guilt on recall, but 'Body as Enemy' and especially the globally externalized appraisal 'Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you' shift toward current somatic threat/general danger beliefs that are not reflected in the memory content and are hard to reconcile with the otherwise memory-centred formulation. Given no active Threat or Trigger links, these appraisal items do not align well with the specified cognitive pattern.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: This appraisal is hard to reconcile with the provided cognitive formulation. The only active connections are between Negative Appraisals and Memory, suggesting appraisals should be closely tied to trauma recollection and meaning-making about the event. A generalized interpersonal-danger belief ('You can never know who will harm you') implies an active Threat focus, yet Threat is otherwise unrepresented and all Threat-related edges are inactive. The other appraisal items are self-blaming and memory-linked (weakness, inaction guilt), so this one pulls the profile toward a different formulation not supported elsewhere.

vignette:
Captain Ricardo Vargas presents as a man accustomed to command, his posture rigid and his gaze direct. At 55, he has dedicated his life to the Navy, cultivating an aura of unflappable competence that has served him well through decades of service. It is this carefully constructed identity that has begun to feel like a costume, one he fears will fall away at any moment to reveal the man he has come to believe he truly is. The precipitating event occurred two years ago, not on the deck of a warship, but in the bustling market of a foreign city where he was visiting his sister’s family while on leave. He was walking with his ten-year-old niece, Sofia, the air thick with the scent of grilled meats and exhaust fumes, when a car bomb detonated less than a block away. The blast threw them both to the ground. For a few critical seconds, Ricardo was paralyzed, the world reduced to a high-pitched whine and the acrid taste of dust and cordite in his mouth. In that moment of stunned inaction, he saw Sofia lying a few feet away, her leg twisted at an unnatural angle. He, the trained officer, simply stared, his mind a complete blank.

In the immediate aftermath, Ricardo functioned on autopilot. He could recount the sequence of events—the explosion, the chaos, the scramble to get Sofia to a makeshift clinic—with the unnerving detachment of a man reading an incident report. He described the scene to his family and to officials with a flat, emotionless tone, as if narrating a story that had happened to a stranger. This numbness was a temporary shield. Back at his post in San Diego, the memories began to break through the dam. The triggers were mundane, unpredictable. The sharp clang of a dropped tool on the steel floor of the maintenance bay, the sudden blare of a ship’s horn cutting through the fog—each sound could send him back. When the memory came, it was never just a thought; it was a full sensory immersion. He would be standing in his office but smelling the market’s smoke, feeling the grit of debris on his teeth, and hearing the piercing screams that followed the blast.

With these vivid intrusions came a suffocating wave of guilt. He would see Sofia’s terrified face and be consumed by the memory of his own hesitation. He was certain that a better man, a stronger man, would have reacted instantly, shielding her, protecting her. This belief has since calcified into a core truth: he is a weak person who failed in his most fundamental duty. He will never forgive himself for not doing more, for not being the protector he was supposed to be. This self-appraisal has reshaped his life. He began avoiding the very environments where he once thrived. He volunteered for desk duty, trading the dynamic environment of the naval yard for the quiet predictability of administrative work, all to minimize the chance of encountering a sudden, loud noise. He and his partner, Elena, used to enjoy crowded street fairs and concerts, but he now finds excuses to stay home, the press of a crowd and the cacophony of sounds being too reminiscent of the market. The silence between them has grown, as he cannot bear to speak of his experience, convinced that sharing the truth of his inaction would only confirm his weakness in her eyes. It was Elena who finally insisted he seek help, telling him, "I feel like you're lost at sea, and you won't let me send a lifeline." Ricardo has come to therapy not with hope, but with a quiet desperation, terrified of having his profound failure seen by another, yet unable to continue living as the ghost in his own decorated uniform.
